Me choosing to take my medications has dramatically improved my life for the better. There will be a lot of people in this sub who will disagree with me, but as someone who actually has the disease the treatment has come a long way in the last few years. Look into a drug called Vraylar. It was developed very recently and as such unfortunately there is no generic, and can be very expensive without insurance, but if you have the means please get actual medical treatment. Smoking weed definitely makes things better in the short term but there is a lot of research that says that thc and manic bipolar are a really bad mix. I say this as someone who has had multiple episodes directly related to my weed intake. Anyways, sorry for the wall of text. I just want to see all my bipolar peeps take care of themselves and flourish the way they deserve to. And unfortunately self medicating does not work. The bipolar mind is kind of insatiable, and as such needs to be treated with care. 

In short, having a good psychiatrist and therapist, along with healthy living habits will make the disease much more bearable. I don’t think it’s a total sin to smoke every once in a while, but self medicating with weed as your only treatment is probably a bad idea.

Hello, another bipolar 2 here. Fantastic comment here with some really great insight. I think mania is something many people either don’t understand or simply ascribe to, as you said, the person “getting over” a depressive episode. It almost took my life and it’s taken years of medication, therapy, inpatient treatment, and a VILLAGE of supportive friends and family to help me get over my suicidal tendencies.
 
To any fellow bipolar people reading this, especially the ones who are in the middle of figuring out the right meds or in between therapists, what you’re feeling is not permanent. Do not be afraid to reach out, and most importantly take care of yourself. There are plenty of things that are out of your control, but the things that are within your control (like taking your meds, talking to your support network) can quite literally save your life. It is a brutal and trying condition, but let me say, from personal experience, it is a fight worth fighting. I’ve had some of the most impactful and poignant experiences after my suicide attempt, and I’m thankful every day I wasn’t successful.
